channel.title: Claroc Blog
channel.description: What the Claroc team is learning about AI‑built apps, the SaaS your company actually runs, and the access it hands out.

item.title: GhostShares 2: Grok Apps Exposed xAI’s Business Secrets and People’s Private Data
item.description: We found more than 35,000 apps built with Grok that anyone with the link could open. Among them were SpaceXSI's own sales territory map, an X ad proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential, an ICU patient's lab results, a hospital group's staff list and a timesheet that hands out its employees' passwords.

item.title: Railway security incident: finding the apps your employees deployed
item.description: On October 21, 2026, Railway asked every customer to revoke all environment variables stored on its platform. This post covers what Railway disclosed and what its users reported in the first hours, and shows how security teams can find the apps and keys they need to rotate.

item.title: GhostShares: A Shared Muse Chat Exposed Prep for a Confidential Call With a Frontier AI Lab Leader
item.description: When someone asks Meta's Muse AI assistant to share a conversation, Muse publishes it as a page anyone with the link can open. That is by design: a public link is the only way the teammate it is sent to can open it. Claroc's research team found these links are also easy to find without ever being given them, because passive-DNS and subdomain-discovery tools list the hostnames directly. Opening a sample in incognito, with no login, revealed people's personal files and companies' internal documents: a home-sale budget, a to-do note flagging a bank-fraud alert with a partial account number, a small-business loan application, a CEO-only revenue review, and a candidate's confidential prep for an executive-search call with a frontier AI lab. On October 20, 2026, after Ars Technica asked about these findings, Meta said it is suspending the feature.

item.title: LinkDrift: How Leaked Links Exposed Internal Files at Fortune 500 Companies
item.description: The links had already leaked. The files were still accessible. We followed URLs from malware logs and public indexes to sensitive corporate material, without a login.
